# THEORYs with `tags` `databases`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Databases and data structures** — how stored data is organized so that it can be found and kept current — physical database design and index selection, materialized views and the choice of which answers to precompute, adaptive and self-organizing structures, lower bounds on lookup, caching and paging; and the cost of organizing ahead of use against organizing in use. Read for itself, not as ML practice: learned indexes and other machine-learning approaches go to the anthology (ADR-045).

| [THEORY-332](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-332.md) v2 | For one index with no space limit, Bruno and Chaudhuri's online tuner, which builds the index once the savings it would have given have risen by its build cost above their last low and drops it once they have fallen by the build cost below their last high, is not three-competitive: when every statement's saving or loss is at most a fraction f of the build cost, a repeated workload makes it cost nearly 3 + 2f times the offline optimum, and one statement whose saving exceeds the build cost makes the ratio unbounded; no upper bound is shown | Bruno and Chaudhuri (2007), [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md), read in [NOTE-896](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-896.md). An always-on index tuner keeps, per index, the running sum of what each statement would have saved (updates counting as losses) and creates or drops the index when that sum moves by the build cost from its last extreme. The paper calls the single-index rule three-competitive, but its proof is one workload on which the ratio approaches 3, a lower bound. The reading's own check found ratios up to 4.7 when one statement's saving is near the build cost, and an unbounded ratio when it exceeds it; with every saving at most a tenth of the build cost no random workload passed 2.4, but a constructed one with steps at most fB approaches 3 + 2f (note of 2026-10-20). The multi-index tuner with a space limit is heuristic, and all costs are optimizer estimates. | Active |
| [THEORY-333](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-333.md) | Database cracking, which partitions a copy of a column in place as a side effect of each range query, measured in memory on 10^7 integers under uniformly random ranges, costs about 40% more than a scan on the first query and far less than sorting, gets cheaper per query with use, and stays cumulatively cheaper than sort-then-search until about 10^5 queries; that only the queried ranges get organized is not tested | Idreos, Kersten and Manegold (2007), [LIT-1090](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1090.md), read in [NOTE-892](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-892.md). Each range select splits, in place, the pieces of a column copy that hold its bounds and records the boundaries in an AVL tree, so later queries touch only edge pieces. In MonetDB on 10^7 values the first such select took 0.38 s against 0.27 s for a scan and about 3.3 s for sort-then-search, later selects 10 to 100 microseconds, and sorting overtook cracking in total only after about 10^5 queries. Every workload is uniformly random, so the paper's claim that only ranges of interest get organized is asserted from the mechanism, not measured; there is no cost model and no rule for when a reorganization pays. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-338](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-338.md) | For a list searched from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each found item to the front costs at most twice what any rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the future (four times counting its own moves), a fixed order by access frequency is within no constant factor, and paying to rearrange ahead of need never helps; for paging, no online rule beats the offline optimum by less than n/(n − n_MIN + 1), and LRU meets that bound | Sleator and Tarjan (1985), [LIT-1093](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1093.md), read in [NOTE-903](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-903.md). With no probabilistic assumption, move-to-front on a sequentially scanned list is within 2 of the best algorithm in its class on every sequence, the rival being free to rearrange as it goes and to know the whole future; a list sorted once by frequency, transpose and frequency count are not within any constant; and any algorithm can be replaced by one no more expensive that makes no paid rearrangement (Theorem 3). For paging the online price of not knowing the future is n/(n − n_MIN + 1), the size of fast memory when the memories are equal. | [THEORY-340](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-340.md) | For answering membership in a static set of n keys with the fewest worst-case cell reads, sorted order with binary search is optimal only when the key universe exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold and table cells may hold nothing but stored keys or pointer symbols; it is beaten for small universes, and by two probes once one cell may hold an encoded value | Yao (1981), [LIT-1097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1097.md), read in [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md). | [THEORY-341](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-341.md) | Inferring not-P from failure to prove P is a deduction only under two separate conditions: Clark shows that when every branch of the search for a proof of P ends in failure, not-P is a theorem of the completed database, and a search that does not finish licenses nothing; Reiter's closed-world assumption, adding the negation of every ground atom the database does not entail, keeps a consistent Horn database consistent and can make a disjunctive one inconsistent | Clark (1978), [LIT-1087](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1087.md), read in [NOTE-894](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-894.md), and Reiter (1978), [LIT-1088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1088.md), read in [NOTE-899](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-899.md) from his 1977 workshop report. | [THEORY-344](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-344.md) | An access method's read, update and memory overheads, each a ratio to the base data alone with a floor of 1.0, are conjectured to trade so that bounding any two forces a lower bound on the third; the conjecture is unproved, its formal wording says no more than the floor already does, and the paper's extreme designs show conflicts between pairs, read against memory and update against read, not a symmetric three-way trade | Athanassoulis et al. | [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) | Choosing indexes for a known mix of queries and updates, to minimize query cost plus a per-index upkeep, is NP-hard as the number of attributes and query types grows, and the tools built for it choose one stored order and a set of secondary indexes per table by searching configurations costed with the query optimizer's own estimates, optimal at best relative to those estimates, with no proved guarantee for their heuristics and no term for the one-time cost of building | Piatetsky-Shapiro (1983), [LIT-1089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1089.md), read in [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md); Finkelstein, Schkolnick and Tiberio (1988), [LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md), read in [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md); Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md), read in [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md). The model is steady state over a fixed workload: it prices upkeep against per-query savings, not a one-off build or sort against later lookups, and its optimality is relative to the optimizer's estimates, never to measured execution. | Active |
| [THEORY-348](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-348.md) | When staying in one state costs a fixed amount per request and leaving it costs a fixed one-time price, switching once the extra cost paid for staying equals that price is within 2 of the offline optimum on every request sequence, and no deterministic online rule does better; with a third option the best guaranteed ratio rises to 3 | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph and Sleator (1988), [LIT-1096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1096.md), read in [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md). It is the first competitive analysis of a rent-or-buy decision, though the paper never uses the name, and its instance is when to stop maintaining a copy. Prices are fixed and known, the guarantee is worst case only, stale reads are forbidden rather than priced, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Active |
| [THEORY-350](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-350.md) | Under a budget on maintenance time, a stored view's upkeep depends on which other views are stored, so upkeep is not additive and adding a view can lower it, and greedily adding the single view of best saving per unit of upkeep can be arbitrarily bad; on OR view graphs a greedy over inverted tree sets gets 1 − 1/e of the saving of an optimum given as much upkeep, using up to twice the budget, if no tree-piece of the optimum alone exceeds the budget | Gupta and Mumick (1999), [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md), read in [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md), with the proofs of the journal version (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md), and the superadditivity first noted by Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md). Grouping views into inverted tree sets restores a 1 − 1/e guarantee, proved in 2005 (Theorem 8), for OR view graphs only, bicriteria, under an assumption on the optimum, with greedy stages exponential in general. The proof does not treat the negative effective costs the paper allows. Upkeep is a budget, not a cost traded against savings, and staleness and build cost are not modelled. | Active |
| [THEORY-356](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-356.md) | When stored views are never updated, greedily storing the view of largest marginal saving in query cost gets at least 1 − 1/e of the optimal saving on a data-cube lattice or any OR or AND view graph, against the optimum for the same number of views or for the space the greedy ends up using, which may exceed the budget by one view | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md), read in [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md); Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md); Gupta and Mumick (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md). | [THEORY-361](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-361.md) | When every object but one has full grade in exactly one of two attribute-sorted lists and the one has full grade in both, finding it under min takes at least about half the objects' worth of accesses for any algorithm that only reads the lists from the top and looks up objects already seen, and, with the tied objects in random order, about as many in expectation even for algorithms that may look up any object; a query on one attribute alone costs k accesses whatever the number of objects | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): Example 6.3 and Theorem 6.4, the paper's proof that no algorithm is instance optimal once lucky lookups are allowed. | [THEORY-362](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-362.md) v2 | For nonrecursive Datalog or SQL views with safe stratified negation and stratified aggregation, under set or duplicate semantics, storing with each derived tuple only the number of its derivations suffices to maintain the view under insertions and deletions of base tuples: signed counts propagated through delta rules stratum by stratum give each tuple's change as its new count minus its old, a tuple leaves when its count reaches zero, and a MIN or MAX group whose extreme is deleted is recomputed from the stored lower stratum | Gupta, Mumick and Subrahmanian (1993), [LIT-1114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1114.md), read in [NOTE-915](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-915.md). | [THEORY-363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-363.md) | For finding the top k objects under a monotone combining function from m lists each sorted by one attribute, with sorted and random accesses the only costs, the threshold algorithm is correct and on every database costs at most a constant times what any correct algorithm that makes no wild guesses costs; the constant is m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, no deterministic algorithm does better when the function is strict, and once wild guesses are allowed no algorithm has such a guarantee on databases with ties | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). | [THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md) | When each cached value is an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, and a query must return an answer interval no wider than R whatever the true values, choosing the cheapest set of exact reads for a SUM is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and solved by taking the narrowest intervals first when read costs are equal, and for a COUNT with a selection predicate the cheapest choice is the ⌈\|T?\| − R⌉ cheapest undecided tuples | Olston and Widom (2000), [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md), read in [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md). | [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v2 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. For the graphs it does build, cost no worse than logarithmic is measured on uniform random data at d = 8, a saturating beam width at d = 4, and at d = 128 (200M SIFT) the growth departs from a logarithm. | [THEORY-367](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-367.md) v2 | For SPJU relational queries, which Buneman, Khanna and Tan's tree model encodes, the minimal witnesses of an output tuple, the inclusion-minimal sets of source facts from which the query still derives it, are the minimal sets matched by single derivations and so are the same for every equivalent query, while where-provenance, the source location a value was copied from, can differ between equivalent queries | Buneman, Khanna and Tan (2001), [LIT-1104](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1104.md), read in [NOTE-920](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-920.md). | [THEORY-368](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-368.md) | On two-dimensional point sets constructed for the purpose, DiskANN as implemented, HNSW, NSG and seven other graph indexes, run from their authors' code at their authors' parameters, found none or few of a query's five nearest neighbours until the search queue held about 10% of the points, for n from 10⁵ to 2·10⁶; this is shown by experiment on one query per instance, and no theorem bounds these algorithms | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). | [THEORY-369](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-369.md) v2 | Under uniformly distributed, independent data and queries in the unit cube with Euclidean distance and a fixed number of points, an optimal nearest-neighbour search over any index that partitions points into blocks or convex clusters of at least two points must read a fraction of blocks that grows toward all of them as dimension rises; with a five-fold sequential advantage for scanning, estimates put the crossover at about 15–26 dimensions for rectangular and spherical bounding regions, and two tree indexes measured on 50,000 points lost to a scan beyond about 10 | Weber, Schek and Blott (1998), [LIT-1107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1107.md), read in [NOTE-919](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-919.md). | [THEORY-371](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-371.md) | For conjunctive queries without equality or comparisons, two queries are equivalent exactly when homomorphisms run both ways between the queries read as small databases, every such query has a minimal equivalent query unique up to isomorphism obtained by deleting atoms, and evaluating one against a database is NP-complete when the query is part of the input | Chandra and Merlin (1977), [LIT-1111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1111.md), read in [NOTE-907](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-907.md). | [THEORY-372](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-372.md) | For c-approximate near-neighbour search over n points in Euclidean space, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} are achievable on any data set whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming space), and no list-of-points structure, the model of known data-independent hashing, does better on random instances; without that model the curve is matched only at query time n^{o(1)} by one or two cell probes | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten (2017), [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md), read in [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) from the arXiv full version. | [THEORY-373](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-373.md) | For positive relational algebra on relations whose tuples are annotated from a commutative semiring, every query's annotated answer equals its answer over provenance polynomials N[X] in the input tuple ids, evaluated at the input annotations, so set, bag, c-table and event-table semantics all factor through the polynomials; revaluing inputs can remove output tuples but never add them, and nothing is shown for negation, difference or aggregation | Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen (2007), [LIT-1110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1110.md), read in [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md). With semantic regions as the unit of eviction, Manhattan distance from the most recent query beat LRU at every query size on a skewed selection workload, and a directional variant was best or tied on random map paths (LRU within 1.06) and on lollipop paths circling a square five or more times; MRU won on a single circuit and on plain squares (Manhattan 2.29 and LRU 9.57 on the 32 × 32 square). The study is simulation only, with synthetic paths and no refetch cost in any value; it shows that the best forecast of reuse depends on the workload, not that semantic distance is a robust rule. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-376](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-376.md) | In a simulated single-client, read-only database answering selection queries on one relation, describing cached data by the predicates of past queries let each query be answered partly from cache, with only the remainder Q ∧ ¬V sent to the server, which matched page caching under good clustering, beat it under bad clustering and answered over 60% of small queries without contacting the server; the cost of computing probe and remainder queries was not charged | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava and Tan (1996), [LIT-1113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1113.md), read in [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md). In one simulator (one client, one server, a 10,000-tuple relation, 90% of queries in a hot 10%), semantic caching performed about like page caching on a clustered index, far better on an unclustered one, and on an unindexed attribute answered over 60% of 1% queries with no server scan. Space overhead depended on coalescing: 55 regions and about 275 factors for 1% queries without it. The result is measured, not proved; updates, joins and the CPU cost of reasoning about the cache's contents were left out, so it does not show that predicate-described storage pays when finding the reusable part is costly. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-377](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-377.md) v2 | In Olston, Loo and Widom's simulations, a rule that multiplies a cached interval's width by 1 + α on a pushed refresh with probability min{ρ, 1}, and divides it by 1 + α on a query's exact fetch with probability min{1/ρ, 1}, settled within 1% of the best fixed width on one random walk and within 5% over eight walk settings; on a 50-host network-traffic trace, restricted to exact copies, it almost matched a tuned adaptive cache-or-not rule, and with a 50-value cache, where queries tolerated imprecision, it cost less; that it converges to the best width is argued, not proved | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The rule treats a pushed refresh as "too narrow" and a fetch as "too wide", weighted by ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and needs no measurement of update rates, query rates or precision demands. Within 1% of the best fixed width on one random walk and within 5% over eight settings; with α = 1 and thresholds it tracked a 50-host traffic trace. With every copy forced exact it decided cache-or-not as well as an adaptive exact-caching rule, and did better where imprecision was allowed, except with a small cache. Convergence is argued from the balance condition only, all evidence is the authors' simulation, and there is no worst-case guarantee. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
| [THEORY-379](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-379.md) | When the orderings of m attribute-sorted lists of N objects are probabilistically independent, Fagin's Algorithm finds the top k objects under any monotone combining function with O(N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m)) accesses with arbitrarily high probability, and for strict combining functions no correct algorithm does essentially better in the worst case with high probability; without independence the bound is not claimed | Fagin (1996/1999), [LIT-1108](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1108.md), as reported by Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). Fagin's own paper could not be obtained, and the reporting paper declines to describe the probability model ("off track"). It does correct one misreading: the only probabilistic assumption is independence of the lists' orderings, not a uniform distribution of grades. For two lists the bound is √(Nk). It does not hold for anti-correlated attributes, where any algorithm can need about half the objects. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-380](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-380.md) v2 | For datalog over a finite input instance annotated from a commutative ω-continuous semiring, with an answer's tag defined as the sum over its derivation trees of the product of its leaves' tags, the tags are the least fixed point of a finite polynomial system and factor through formal power series N∞⟦X⟧ in the input tuple ids; an answer tuple's series has an infinite coefficient exactly when one of its derivation trees contains a tuple lying on a cycle of unit rules | Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen (2007), [LIT-1110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1110.md), read in [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md). A recursive query can derive a tuple in infinitely many ways, so polynomials do not suffice and the semiring needs infinite sums. With ω-continuous semirings and the provenance semiring N∞⟦X⟧ the paper states the analogues of the relational results: a fixed-point characterization (Theorem 5.6), factorization (Theorem 6.4), and a test for infinite coefficients (Theorem 6.5), with algorithms that decide finiteness and compute coefficients. Proofs are not given. Plain N and N[X] are excluded, the provenance can be an infinite object held only as equations, and negation remains outside. | Active |
| [THEORY-381](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-381.md) | In the cell-probe model, a near-neighbour structure on n random points that answers in t probes with m cells of w bits must satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ the robust expansion of the metric's neighbourhood graph at measure 1/m^t (and (mwt/n)^t ≥ its vertex expansion if deterministic), so in expanding spaces such as the hypercube fast queries need space polynomially larger than the data; the bounds are average case, approximate, and fall off exponentially in t | Panigrahy, Talwar and Wieder (2010), [LIT-1102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1102.md), read in [NOTE-914](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-914.md) from the arXiv preprint. For graphical neighbour search, to which decision approximate near neighbour reduces, on data drawn so that neighbourhoods rarely overlap: deterministic t-probe structures satisfy (mwt/n)^t ≥ Φv and m^t·t·w/n ≥ Φv(1/m^t); randomized ones satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ Φr(1/m^t, γ/t) and (mwt⁴/n)^{2t} ≥ Φr(1/m, γ/t). On the hypercube this gives space n^{1+Ω(1/(ct))} at approximation c and n^{Ω(1/(tε²))} at 1 + ε; a one-probe structure matches on Cayley graphs; low-contention dynamic structures need update time at least Φr(τ, 1/(4t²)) over poly(t). Tight only for constant t; nothing about worst-case or structured data, workloads or build time. | Active |
| [THEORY-382](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-382.md) v2 | When a web server keeps each page fragment either cached and invalidated by updates or stored and refreshed after them, materializing trades staleness for response time, and in one synthetic simulation with fixed costs a periodic greedy that moves a capped number of fragments between the two, to keep the share of fresh fragments served above a set threshold, tracked that threshold by the authors' reading of its curves, answered faster than caching alone and recovered from overload by materializing everything; no bound on its distance from the best plan is shown | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2003), [LIT-1105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1105.md), read in [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md). Quality of Data is the share of fresh fragments in served pages; OVIS(θ) estimates per fragment the change in response time (hits and misses against refresh load) and in QoD from switching policy, and each period greedily switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments to spend a QoD surplus on speed or buy back a deficit. The paper asserts the greedy step is best under the cap and proves nothing; the evidence is one simulator with uniform costs and no comparison with an optimum. The reading the evidence does not support: that this is a joint cost model of build, upkeep, staleness and savings. Staleness is a user-set threshold, not a price, and switching and storage are free. | Active |
| [THEORY-383](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-383.md) | On one Apache and Informix server answering cheap indexed selections, a page whose query result was stored in the DBMS and refreshed on every update answered more slowly than one recomputed on each request whenever updates arrived, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it and its refresh loaded the same DBMS, while a finished page stored at the web server and rewritten on every update answered 10 to 230 times faster than either | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2000), [LIT-1118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1118.md), read in [NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md). Three ways to serve a database-generated page under online updates, with no stale reads allowed: compute on request, store the query result in the DBMS, or store the finished page at the web server. A cost model sums access and update costs by frequency; the per-page selection problem is stated and not solved. On their testbed the page stored at the web server won at every load, and the result stored in the DBMS lost to recomputation once there were updates. The reading the evidence does not support: that storing an answer pays whenever it is reused enough. Where it is stored decided the outcome, and the generalization to other systems is the authors' expectation, not a measurement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-384](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-384.md) | A nearest-neighbour graph built by pruning each point's links against all other points with a factor α > 1, so that from every point some link is α times closer to any other point, lets greedy search from any start reach a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by one on n, and the build takes O(n³) time done naively | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). Proved for DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" build, not the build DiskANN implements. The guarantee rests on one property of the graph (α-shortcut reachability, α > 1), gives a constant approximation, not exact search, is logarithmic in the aspect ratio ∆, which can exceed n by far, and has a per-step cost exponential in the doubling dimension. HNSW and NSG prune with α = 1 and are not covered. | Active |
| [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) | In a proximity-graph index over data in isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves greedy search stuck at cluster boundaries and short of high recall, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already chosen keeps the clusters connected and search fast; on uniform or very high-dimensional data the two rules differ little, and the evidence is the authors' own tests on synthetic and benchmark data | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md) | When a cached interval of width W is kept valid by its source, which pushes a refresh at cost C_vr whenever the value leaves it, and queries fetch the exact value at cost C_qr whenever it is too wide, and the chances of the two per step go as 1/W² and as W, the expected refresh cost is least at W* = (ρK₁/K₂)^(1/3) with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, where ρ times the chance of a pushed refresh equals the chance of a fetch | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The cost rate Ω(W) = C_vr·K₁/W² + C_qr·K₂·W is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr. The minimum is calculus on assumed forms. P_qr ∝ W follows exactly from uniform precision demands; P_vr ∝ 1/W² comes from a Chebyshev bound on a random walk used as an estimate, and the paper's simulation of a random walk measured both proportionalities. Staleness here is priced as refresh traffic: the source guarantees validity, so a stale read is imprecise but never wrong, and there is no build cost and no cost of a wrong or imprecise answer. | Active |
| [THEORY-387](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-387.md) v2 | For positive recursive Datalog views under set semantics, deleting every derived tuple that has any derivation through a deleted base fact, then restoring each deleted tuple that still has a derivation from what remains, then adding what insertions derive, leaves exactly the tuples derivable from the new base (E − Δ⁻) ∪ Δ⁺, with no derivation counts stored; the extension to stratified negation and aggregation is asserted, not shown, and the size of the overestimate is not measured | Gupta, Mumick and Subrahmanian (1993), [LIT-1114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1114.md), read in [NOTE-915](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-915.md). DRed runs stratum by stratum: semi-naive Δ⁻-rules compute an overestimate of deletions, δ⁺-rules put back those with a derivation in the reduced database, and Δ⁺-rules add insertions. Theorem 7.1 states the result contains t if and only if t has a derivation in (E − Δ⁻) ∪ Δ⁺; the proof is in a 1992 AT&T report the record has not seen. The paper asserts, and does not show, that DRed handles stratified negation, aggregation and rule changes, that it beats the PF algorithm by up to an order of magnitude, and that it is slower than counting on nonrecursive views. | Active |
| [THEORY-388](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-388.md) | Locality-sensitive hashing answers approximate near-neighbour queries over n points with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, where ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) is set by how much more often near pairs collide than far ones and is at most 1/(1+ε) for approximation 1+ε in Hamming space, with constant success probability per query; the paper gives upper bounds only and proves no limit on what organizing can buy | Indyk and Motwani (1998), [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md), read in [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) from the authors' 1999 expanded version, compared with the STOC text. A hash family under which points within r1 collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond r2 with at most p2 gives n^ρ random tables, each storing every point: O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), for the decision version, which ring-cover trees connect to approximate nearest neighbour with polylog overhead. Bit sampling gives ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in Hamming space and, by embedding, ℓ_p for p in [1, 2]; the STOC text states 1/ε and only for ε > 1. Grid bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Preprocessing is counted as space. Nothing is proved about whether these exponents can be beaten. | Active |
| [THEORY-389](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-389.md) | For conjunctive queries and views without comparison predicates, a stored view can be used in an equivalent rewriting of a query exactly when the view's body maps homomorphically into the query's, a minimal rewriting needs no more literals than the query, and deciding whether a rewriting shorter than the query or one using only the views exists is NP-complete in the size of the query and view definitions; with comparisons in both, deciding whether any rewriting uses the views is Π2p-complete | Levy, Mendelzon, Sagiv and Srivastava (1995), [LIT-1100](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1100.md), read in [NOTE-909](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-909.md). Every use of a view in an equivalent rewriting comes from a containment mapping from the view into the query (Proposition 3.1); without comparisons a locally minimal complete rewriting has at most as many literals as the query (Lemma 3.5), which puts the problems in NP, and they are NP-complete (Theorems 3.7, 3.9, 3.10), with two independent sources of hardness. The results are worst case, in the size of the definitions rather than the stored data, for equivalent rewritings under set semantics only; they do not say recognizing reuse is costly in practice, and they do not cover contained (partial) rewritings. | Active |
